newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary's BUX jumps to new record, bucks Euro mkts.
newsitem.headline: Hungary's BUX jumps to new record, bucks Euro mkts.

text.p: 1125 GMT - The Hungarian share market bucked bearish European markets and moved higher reaching a new record level on Friday as fresh funds flew into the bourse, traders said.
* The BUX index finished at 6,018.11 points, up 88.96 points or 1.50 percent.
* Seventeen stocks ended higher, nine lower and eight steady.
The Hungarian share market bucked the falling trend on European markets and rallied to a new record high on Friday, traders said.
"Friday's rise caused surprise, people expected a calm session," said Robert Forgo of MKB Securities.
The BUX index finished at 6,018.11 points, up 88.96 points or 1.50 percent, after a slow start.
Traders attributed the sudden rise to an inflow of fresh funds to the Budapest bourse, which seems to be one destination for money leaving the troubled Czech markets.

"Money suddenly started to flow in from abroad," Forgo said, adding that this drove the BUX index to close over the 6,000 point level for the first time. Earlier this week the indicator rose to an intra-day high of 6,012.20 points.

"Money shifts over to Hungary because of problems on the Czech markets," said Forgo, adding that one further reason might be that investors digested the first quarter earnings and now decided to move into the market.
Gyorgy Czipo of ING Barings said: "There was fresh money as some shifted from the Czech market."
Nevertheless, turnover was not particularly strong, with slightly over one million shares and compensation coupons trading.

"Most of the investors in central Europe are turning their eyes to problems in the Czech Republic," said James Oates, director for central and eastern Europe at UBS in London. "The crisis is getting much bigger."
"The result is that most people therefore are trying to change their positions in the Czech Republic and they are not really focusing on Hungary."
On Friday, the coupons gained the most in percentage term, adding almost seven percent to finish at 670 forints.

As for shares, the few losers included the less liquid papers but also retailer Fotex whose shareholders on Thursday decided to cancel two convertible bond issues to existing shareholders, planned for September 1997 and March 1998. Fotex ended at 140 forints, down five.
Elsewhere on the market, chemicals BorsodChem, rated by Hungary's OTP Securities as "hold", ended at 6,700 forints, up 120.
Despite Friday's gain, analysts said the market's outlook was flat.
"We can expect a fairly sideways, not very exciting market over the next week or so while people try to understand what has actually happened in Prague," UBS's Oates said.
"There will be little activity from foreigners because they're going to be concerned about what's happening in Prague."
-- Emese Bartha, Budapest newsroom +36 1 327-4040
